newsitem.title: JAPAN: Poitier becomes the Bahamas ambassador to Japan.
newsitem.headline: Poitier becomes the Bahamas ambassador to Japan.

text.p: Hollywood star Sidney Poitier took on a new role on Wednesday, representing the Bahamas as ambassador to Japan.
The 70-year-old Oscar-winning actor, who holds dual U.S. and Bahamian nationality, took up the post in a ceremony presided over by Japanese Emperor Akihito at the Imperial Palace.
"It's exhilarating, it's a very satisfying feeling," he told Reuters in an interview after formally presenting his credentials to the emperor.
Poitier, who has only visited Japan twice before and has no plans to live here, will carry out his duties while continuing to make movies around the world.

"There will be times when I will make films, there will be times when I will probably direct films. There will be no time when I'm not available to fulfil my responsibilities as an ambassador," he said.
It's just as well Poitier is not planning to live in Tokyo since the 700-island Caribbean nation has no embassy in Japan.
He said it was important to him to help promote the country where he grew up and which was the home of his parents and forefathers.

"I was raised in the Bahamas. My roots are there. I am as familiar with that society and its people as I am with America and there is in the present government a need for me to be of some service," he said.
Expressing admiration for Japan as an industrious nation with a remarkable culture, Poitier said he wanted to see more Japanese people enjoying the Bahamas.

Speaking about his latest movie, "Mandela and de Klerk", a television film for the U.S. Showtime Channel in which he stars with Michael Caine, Poitier said it was a once in a lifetime opportunity to play Nelson Mandela.
"We have watched this incredible personality mature into a force that words cannot describe. So playing him as an opportunity was just great," he said.

In response to criticism from South African actors that the role should have gone to a South African, he said there were many excellent South African actors who could have played the role just as well but the film needed an actor well-known overseas to make it financially viable.

Poitier's movies include "Guess Who's Coming to Dinner?" in 1968, one of the first Hollywood films to examine interracial marriage. He was the first black actor to win an Oscar, for the 1963 movie "Lilies of the Field".
